content:
Hoists can protect both the person and carers.

This guide covers the conversation. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why a hoist

Lifting someone by hand can injure them and the carer.

Assessment and training

  • An occupational therapist assesses.
  • Carers need training before use.

Dignity

Involve the person in decisions.

Support for carers

Ask for a carer's assessment.

When to get help

  • Call 999 or go to A&E if someone suddenly becomes confused. Many causes need immediate assessment. Do not assume it is a urine infection, dementia or a medicine effect. Do not drive yourself to A&E; ask someone else to drive or call 999. Stay with the person and reassure them while help is arranged.
  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for a sudden drop in mobility or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Where does the hoist come from?

Usually council equipment services.

Is it permanent?

Needs can change; ask for review.

Sources and further reading

Living With Arthritis is an independent charity and is not part of Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis). Everyone's situation is different, so follow the advice of your own GP and care team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
